props.title: The Wrong Man
props.initialSlug: Innocent musician fights to clear his name in NYC

sections.content: The Wrong Man stands as Hitchcock's most stark departure from his typical thriller format. Based on a true story, this haunting docudrama follows Manny Balestrero (Henry Fonda), a jazz musician wrongly accused of robbery. Unlike the glamorous wrong-man scenarios in North by Northwest (1959) or The 39 Steps (1935), Hitchcock strips away all sensationalism to create a crushing portrait of an ordinary man ground down by a callous justice system. The film's documentary-style black and white photography and on-location shooting in New York create an unsettling realism that makes Manny's ordeal feel suffocatingly authentic.

movies.title: Call Northside 777
movies.slug: James Stewart stars in this true story of a reporter working to prove the innocence of a man wrongly imprisoned for murder

sections.content: The film's devastating impact comes from its methodical portrayal of how false accusation destroys not just the accused but their entire family. Rose Balestrero's descent into mental illness, portrayed with heartbreaking precision by Vera Miles, represents the collateral damage of wrongful prosecution. This theme of justice system casualties would later influence films like In Cold Blood (1967) and The Hurricane (1999), though few achieve the intimate devastation of Hitchcock's approach.

Hitchcock's decision to shoot in actual locations where the real case occurred - including the actual Stork Club and the Queens courthouse - set a precedent for true-crime filmmaking that influenced works like Dog Day Afternoon (1975) and Serpico (1973). The director's trademark cameo appears in the film's opening minutes, but it's his only concession to style over substance in this remarkably restrained work. SUBHEAD: Documentary Style and Legal System Critique

movies.title: Boomerang
movies.slug: Another true story of wrongful accusation, with Dana Andrews as a prosecutor who begins to doubt his case against a murder suspect

sections.content: The film's influence on later docudrama techniques can't be overstated. Its methodical attention to procedural detail and use of real locations influenced everything from The Battle of Algiers (1966) to United 93 (2006). The Wrong Man's unflinching look at police lineup procedures, witness identification, and the grinding machinery of the justice system laid groundwork for later procedural critiques like And Justice for All (1979) and The Thin Blue Line (1988).
